15 # Init.Prelude
16 
17 This is the first file in the Lean import hierarchy. It is responsible for setting
18 up basic definitions, most of which Lean already has "built in knowledge" about,
19 so it is important that they be set up in exactly this way. (For example, Lean will
20 use `PUnit` in the desugaring of `do` notation, or in the pattern match compiler.)
21 
22 -/

24 universe u v w

26 /-- Marker for information that has been erased by the code generator. -/
27 unsafe axiom lcErased : Type
28 
29 /-- Marker for type dependency that has been erased by the code generator. -/
30 unsafe axiom lcAny : Type

33 unsafe axiom lcVoid : Type

36 /--
37 The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
38 (a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.
39 
40 Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
41 function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
42 and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
43 knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
44 difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
45 typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
46 expression.
47 -/
48 @[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a
49 
50 /--
51 Function composition, usually written with the infix operator `∘`. A new function is created from
52 two existing functions, where one function's output is used as input to the other.
53 
54 Examples:
55  * `Function.comp List.reverse (List.drop 2) [3, 2, 4, 1] = [1, 4]`
56  * `(List.reverse ∘ List.drop 2) [3, 2, 4, 1] = [1, 4]`
57 -/
58 @[inline] def Function.comp {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {δ : Sort w} (f : β → δ) (g : α → β) : α → δ :=
59   fun x => f (g x)
60 
61 /--
62 The constant function that ignores its argument.
63 
64 If `a : α`, then `Function.const β a : β → α` is the “constant function with value `a`”. For all
65 arguments `b : β`, `Function.const β a b = a`.
66 
67 Examples:
68  * `Function.const Bool 10 true = 10`
69  * `Function.const Bool 10 false = 10`
70  * `Function.const String 10 "any string" = 10`
71 -/
72 @[inline] def Function.const {α : Sort u} (β : Sort v) (a : α) : β → α :=
73   fun _ => a
74 
75 /--
76 `letFun v (fun x => b)` is a function version of `have x := v; b`.
77 This is equal to `(fun x => b) v`, so the value of `x` is not accessible to `b`.
78 This is in contrast to `let x := v; b`, where the value of `x` is accessible to `b`.
79 
80 This used to be the way `have`/`let_fun` syntax was encoded,
81 and there used to be special support for `letFun` in WHNF and `simp`.
82 -/
83 def letFun {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} (v : α) (f : (x : α) → β x) : β v := f v

86 /--
87 `inferInstance` synthesizes a value of any target type by typeclass
88 inference. This function has the same type signature as the identity
89 function, but the square brackets on the `[i : α]` argument means that it will
90 attempt to construct this argument by typeclass inference. (This will fail if
91 `α` is not a `class`.) Example:
92 ```
93 #check (inferInstance : Inhabited Nat) -- Inhabited Nat
94 
95 def foo : Inhabited (Nat × Nat) :=
96   inferInstance
97 
98 example : foo.default = (default, default) :=
99   rfl
100 ```
101 -/
102 abbrev inferInstance {α : Sort u} [i : α] : α := i
103 
104 set_option checkBinderAnnotations false in
105 /-- `inferInstanceAs α` synthesizes an instance of type `α`, transporting it from a
106 definitionally equal type if necessary. This is useful when `α` is definitionally equal to
107 some `α'` for which instances are registered, as it prevents leaking the definition's RHS
108 at lower transparencies.
109 
110 `inferInstanceAs` requires an expected type from context. If you just need to synthesize an
111 instance without transporting between types, use `inferInstance` instead.
112 
113 Example:
114 ```
115 def D := Nat
116 instance : Inhabited D := inferInstanceAs (Inhabited Nat)
117 ```
118 
119 See `Lean.Meta.WrapInstance` for details.
120 -/
121 abbrev «inferInstanceAs» (α : Sort u) [i : α] : α := i
122

124 /--
125 The canonical universe-polymorphic type with just one element.
126 
127 It should be used in contexts that require a type to be universe polymorphic, thus disallowing
128 `Unit`.
129 -/
130 inductive PUnit : Sort u where
131   /-- The only element of the universe-polymorphic unit type. -/
132   | unit : PUnit
133 
134 /--
135 The canonical type with one element. This element is written `()`.
136 
137 `Unit` has a number of uses:
138  * It can be used to model control flow that returns from a function call without providing other
139    information.
140  * Monadic actions that return `Unit` have side effects without computing values.
141  * In polymorphic types, it can be used to indicate that no data is to be stored in a particular
142    field.
143 -/
144 abbrev Unit : Type := PUnit
145 
146 /--
147 The only element of the unit type.
148 
149 It can be written as an empty tuple: `()`.
150 -/
151 @[match_pattern] abbrev Unit.unit : Unit := PUnit.unit
152 
153 /--
154 Auxiliary unsafe constant used by the Compiler when erasing proofs from code.
155 
156 It may look strange to have an axiom that says "every proposition is true",
157 since this is obviously unsound, but the `unsafe` marker ensures that the
158 kernel will not let this through into regular proofs. The lower levels of the
159 code generator don't need proofs in terms, so this is used to stub the proofs
160 out.
161 -/
162 unsafe axiom lcProof {α : Prop} : α
163 
164 /--
165 Auxiliary unsafe constant used by the Compiler when erasing casts.
166 -/
167 unsafe axiom lcCast {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (a : α) : β
168 
169 
170 /--
171 Auxiliary unsafe constant used by the Compiler to mark unreachable code.
172 
173 Like `lcProof`, this is an `unsafe axiom`, which means that even though it is
174 not sound, the kernel will not let us use it for regular proofs.
175 
176 Executing this expression to actually synthesize a value of type `α` causes
177 **immediate undefined behavior**, and the compiler does take advantage of this
178 to optimize the code assuming that it is not called. If it is not optimized out,
179 it is likely to appear as a print message saying "unreachable code", but this
180 behavior is not guaranteed or stable in any way.
181 -/
182 unsafe axiom lcUnreachable {α : Sort u} : α
183 
184 /--
185 `True` is a proposition and has only an introduction rule, `True.intro : True`.
186 In other words, `True` is simply true, and has a canonical proof, `True.intro`
187 For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
188 -/
189 inductive True : Prop where
190   /-- `True` is true, and `True.intro` (or more commonly, `trivial`)
191   is the proof. -/
192   | intro : True
193 
194 /--
195 `False` is the empty proposition. Thus, it has no introduction rules.
196 It represents a contradiction. `False` elimination rule, `False.rec`,
197 expresses the fact that anything follows from a contradiction.
198 This rule is sometimes called ex falso (short for ex falso sequitur quodlibet),
199 or the principle of explosion.
200 For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
201 -/
202 inductive False : Prop
203 
204 /--
205 The empty type. It has no constructors.
206 
207 Use `Empty.elim` in contexts where a value of type `Empty` is in scope.
208 -/
209 inductive Empty : Type
210 
211 set_option bootstrap.inductiveCheckResultingUniverse false in
212 /--
213 The universe-polymorphic empty type, with no constructors.
214 
215 `PEmpty` can be used in any universe, but this flexibility can lead to worse error messages and more
216 challenges with universe level unification. Prefer the type `Empty` or the proposition `False` when
217 possible.
218 -/
219 inductive PEmpty : Sort u where
220 
221 /--
222 `Not p`, or `¬p`, is the negation of `p`. It is defined to be `p → False`,
223 so if your goal is `¬p` you can use `intro h` to turn the goal into
224 `h : p ⊢ False`, and if you have `hn : ¬p` and `h : p` then `hn h : False`
225 and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.
226 For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
227 -/
228 def Not (a : Prop) : Prop := a → False
229 
230 /--
231 `False.elim : False → C` says that from `False`, any desired proposition
232 `C` holds. Also known as ex falso quodlibet (EFQ) or the principle of explosion.
233 
234 The target type is actually `C : Sort u` which means it works for both
235 propositions and types. When executed, this acts like an "unreachable"
236 instruction: it is **undefined behavior** to run, but it will probably print
237 "unreachable code". (You would need to construct a proof of false to run it
238 anyway, which you can only do using `sorry` or unsound axioms.)
239 -/
240 @[macro_inline] def False.elim {C : Sort u} (h : False) : C :=
241   h.rec
242 
243 /--
244 Anything follows from two contradictory hypotheses. Example:
245 ```
246 example (hp : p) (hnp : ¬p) : q := absurd hp hnp
247 ```
248 For more information: [Propositional Logic](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/propositions_and_proofs.html#propositional-logic)
249 -/
250 @[macro_inline] def absurd {a : Prop} {b : Sort v} (h₁ : a) (h₂ : Not a) : b :=
251   (h₂ h₁).rec
252 
253 /--
254 The equality relation. It has one introduction rule, `Eq.refl`.
255 We use `a = b` as notation for `Eq a b`.
256 A fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation.
257 ```
258 variable (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
259 variable (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)
260 
261 example : a = d :=
262   Eq.trans (Eq.trans hab (Eq.symm hcb)) hcd
263 ```
264 Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has the important property that every assertion
265 respects the equivalence, in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing the truth value.
266 That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution: `Eq.subst h1 h2`.
267 Example:
268 ```
269 example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
270         (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
271   Eq.subst h1 h2
272 
273 example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
274     (h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
275   h1 ▸ h2
276 ```
277 The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of `Eq.subst` and `Eq.symm`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.
278 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
279 -/
280 inductive Eq : α → α → Prop where
281   /-- `Eq.refl a : a = a` is reflexivity, the unique constructor of the
282   equality type. See also `rfl`, which is usually used instead. -/
283   | refl (a : α) : Eq a a
284 
285 /-- Non-dependent recursor for the equality type. -/
286 @[simp] abbrev Eq.ndrec.{u1, u2} {α : Sort u2} {a : α} {motive : α → Sort u1} (m : motive a) {b : α} (h : Eq a b) : motive b :=
287   h.rec m
288 
289 /--
290 `rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
291 same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.
292 
293 This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
294 the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
295 definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
296 Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
297 -/
298 @[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
299 
300 /-- `id x = x`, as a `@[simp]` lemma. -/
301 @[simp] theorem id_eq (a : α) : Eq (id a) a := rfl
302 
303 /--
304 The substitution principle for equality. If `a = b ` and `P a` holds,
305 then `P b` also holds. We conventionally use the name `motive` for `P` here,
306 so that you can specify it explicitly using e.g.
307 `Eq.subst (motive := fun x => x < 5)` if it is not otherwise inferred correctly.
308 
309 This theorem is the underlying mechanism behind the `rw` tactic, which is
310 essentially a fancy algorithm for finding good `motive` arguments to usefully
311 apply this theorem to replace occurrences of `a` with `b` in the goal or
312 hypotheses.
313 
314 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
315 -/
316 theorem Eq.subst {α : Sort u} {motive : α → Prop} {a b : α} (h₁ : Eq a b) (h₂ : motive a) : motive b :=
317   Eq.ndrec h₂ h₁
318 
319 /--
320 Equality is symmetric: if `a = b` then `b = a`.
321 
322 Because this is in the `Eq` namespace, if you have a variable `h : a = b`,
323 `h.symm` can be used as shorthand for `Eq.symm h` as a proof of `b = a`.
324 
325 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
326 -/
327 @[symm] theorem Eq.symm {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : Eq a b) : Eq b a :=
328   h ▸ rfl
329 
330 /-- Non-dependent recursor for the equality type (symmetric variant) -/
331 @[simp] abbrev Eq.ndrec_symm.{u1, u2} {α : Sort u2} {a : α} {motive : α → Sort u1} (m : motive a) {b : α} (h : Eq b a) : motive b :=
332   h.symm.ndrec m
333 
334 /--
335 Equality is transitive: if `a = b` and `b = c` then `a = c`.
336 
337 Because this is in the `Eq` namespace, if you have variables or expressions
338 `h₁ : a = b` and `h₂ : b = c`, you can use `h₁.trans h₂ : a = c` as shorthand
339 for `Eq.trans h₁ h₂`.
340 
341 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
342 -/
343 theorem Eq.trans {α : Sort u} {a b c : α} (h₁ : Eq a b) (h₂ : Eq b c) : Eq a c :=
344   h₂ ▸ h₁
345 
346 /--
347 Cast across a type equality. If `h : α = β` is an equality of types, and
348 `a : α`, then `a : β` will usually not typecheck directly, but this function
349 will allow you to work around this and embed `a` in type `β` as `cast h a : β`.
350 
351 It is best to avoid this function if you can, because it is more complicated
352 to reason about terms containing casts, but if the types don't match up
353 definitionally sometimes there isn't anything better you can do.
354 
355 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
356 -/
357 @[macro_inline] def cast {α β : Sort u} (h : Eq α β) (a : α) : β :=
358   h.rec a
359 
360 /--
361 Congruence in the function argument: if `a₁ = a₂` then `f a₁ = f a₂` for
362 any (nondependent) function `f`. This is more powerful than it might look at first, because
363 you can also use a lambda expression for `f` to prove that
364 `<something containing a₁> = <something containing a₂>`. This function is used
365 internally by tactics like `congr` and `simp` to apply equalities inside
366 subterms.
367 
368 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
369 -/
370 theorem congrArg {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {a₁ a₂ : α} (f : α → β) (h : Eq a₁ a₂) : Eq (f a₁) (f a₂) :=
371   h ▸ rfl
372 
373 /--
374 Congruence in both function and argument. If `f₁ = f₂` and `a₁ = a₂` then
375 `f₁ a₁ = f₂ a₂`. This only works for nondependent functions; the theorem
376 statement is more complex in the dependent case.
377 
378 For more information: [Equality](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/quantifiers_and_equality.html#equality)
379 -/
380 theorem congr {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {f₁ f₂ : α → β} {a₁ a₂ : α} (h₁ : Eq f₁ f₂) (h₂ : Eq a₁ a₂) : Eq (f₁ a₁) (f₂ a₂) :=
381   h₁ ▸ h₂ ▸ rfl
382 
383 /-- Congruence in the function part of an application: If `f = g` then `f a = g a`. -/
384 theorem congrFun {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} {f g : (x : α) → β x} (h : Eq f g) (a : α) : Eq (f a) (g a) :=
385   h ▸ rfl
386 
387 /-- Similar to `congrFun` but `β` does not depend on `α`. -/
388 theorem congrFun' {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} {f g : α → β} (h : Eq f g) (a : α) : Eq (f a) (g a) :=
389   h ▸ rfl

391 /-!
392 Initialize the Quotient Module, which effectively adds the following definitions:
393 ```
394 opaque Quot {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Sort u
395 
396 opaque Quot.mk {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : Quot r
397 
398 opaque Quot.lift {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Sort v} (f : α → β) :
399   (∀ a b : α, r a b → Eq (f a) (f b)) → Quot r → β
400 
401 opaque Quot.ind {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Quot r → Prop} :
402   (∀ a : α, β (Quot.mk r a)) → ∀ q : Quot r, β q
403 ```
404 -/
405 init_quot
406 
407 /--
408 Low-level quotient types. Quotient types coarsen the propositional equality for a type `α`, so that
409 terms related by some relation `r` are considered equal in `Quot r`.
410 
411 Set-theoretically, `Quot r` can seen as the set of equivalence classes of `α` modulo `r`. Functions
412 from `Quot r` must prove that they respect `r`: to define a function `f : Quot r → β`, it is
413 necessary to provide `f' : α → β` and prove that for all `x : α` and `y : α`, `r x y → f' x = f' y`.
414 
415 `Quot` is a built-in primitive:
416  * `Quot.mk` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
417  * `Quot.lift` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
418  * `Quot.sound` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.
419  * `Quot.ind` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
420    with `Quot.mk`.
421 
422 The relation `r` is not required to be an equivalence relation; the resulting quotient type's
423 equality extends `r` to an equivalence as a consequence of the rules for equality and quotients.
424 When `r` is an equivalence relation, it can be more convenient to use the higher-level type
425 `Quotient`.
426 -/
427 add_decl_doc Quot
428 
429 /--
430 Places an element of a type into the quotient that equates terms according to the provided relation.
431 
432 Given `v : α` and relation `r : α → α → Prop`, `Quot.mk r v : Quot r` is like `v`, except all
433 observations of `v`'s value must respect `r`.
434 
435 `Quot.mk` is a built-in primitive:
436  * `Quot` is the built-in quotient type.
437  * `Quot.lift` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
438  * `Quot.sound` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.
439  * `Quot.ind` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
440    with `Quot.mk`.
441 -/
442 add_decl_doc Quot.mk
443 
444 /--
445 A reasoning principle for quotients that allows proofs about quotients to assume that all values are
446 constructed with `Quot.mk`.
447 
448 `Quot.rec` is analogous to the [recursor](lean-manual://section/recursors) for a structure, and can
449 be used when the resulting type is not necessarily a proposition.
450 
451 `Quot.ind` is a built-in primitive:
452  * `Quot` is the built-in quotient type.
453  * `Quot.mk` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
454  * `Quot.lift` allows the definition of functions from the quotient to some other type.
455  * `Quot.sound` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`.
456 -/
457 add_decl_doc Quot.ind
458 
459 /--
460 Lifts a function from an underlying type to a function on a quotient, requiring that it respects the
461 quotient's relation.
462 
463 Given a relation `r : α → α → Prop` and a quotient `Quot r`, applying a function `f : α → β`
464 requires a proof `a` that `f` respects `r`. In this case, `Quot.lift f a : Quot r → β` computes the
465 same values as `f`.
466 
467 Lean's type theory includes a [definitional reduction](lean-manual://section/type-theory) from
468 `Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk r v)` to `f v`.
469 
470 `Quot.lift` is a built-in primitive:
471  * `Quot` is the built-in quotient type.
472  * `Quot.mk` places elements of the underlying type `α` into the quotient.
473  * `Quot.sound` asserts the equality of elements related by `r`
474  * `Quot.ind` is used to write proofs about quotients by assuming that all elements are constructed
475    with `Quot.mk`; it is analogous to the [recursor](lean-manual://section/recursors) for a
476    structure.
477 -/
478 add_decl_doc Quot.lift
479 
480 /--
481 Unsafe auxiliary constant used by the compiler to erase `Quot.lift`.
482 -/
483 unsafe axiom Quot.lcInv {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} (q : Quot r) : α
484 
485 /--
486 Heterogeneous equality. `a ≍ b` asserts that `a` and `b` have the same
487 type, and casting `a` across the equality yields `b`, and vice versa.
488 
489 You should avoid using this type if you can. Heterogeneous equality does not
490 have all the same properties as `Eq`, because the assumption that the types of
491 `a` and `b` are equal is often too weak to prove theorems of interest. One
492 public important non-theorem is the analogue of `congr`: If `f ≍ g` and `x ≍ y`
493 and `f x` and `g y` are well typed it does not follow that `f x ≍ g y`.
494 (This does follow if you have `f = g` instead.) However if `a` and `b` have
495 the same type then `a = b` and `a ≍ b` are equivalent.
496 -/
497 inductive HEq : {α : Sort u} → α → {β : Sort u} → β → Prop where
498   /-- Reflexivity of heterogeneous equality. -/
499   | refl (a : α) : HEq a a
500 
501 /-- A version of `HEq.refl` with an implicit argument. -/
502 @[match_pattern] protected def HEq.rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : HEq a a :=
503   HEq.refl a
504 
505 /-- If two heterogeneously equal terms have the same type, then they are propositionally equal. -/
506 theorem eq_of_heq {α : Sort u} {a a' : α} (h : HEq a a') : Eq a a' :=
507   have : (α β : Sort u) → (a : α) → (b : β) → HEq a b → (h : Eq α β) → Eq (cast h a) b :=
508     fun _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
509       h₁.rec (fun _ => rfl)
510   this α α a a' h rfl
511 
512 /-- Propositionally equal terms are also heterogeneously equal. -/
513 theorem heq_of_eq (h : Eq a a') : HEq a a' :=
514   Eq.subst h (HEq.refl a)
515 
516 /--
517 The product type, usually written `α × β`. Product types are also called pair or tuple types.
518 Elements of this type are pairs in which the first element is an `α` and the second element is a
519 `β`.
520 
521 Products nest to the right, so `(x, y, z) : α × β × γ` is equivalent to `(x, (y, z)) : α × (β × γ)`.
522 -/
523 structure Prod (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
524   /--
525   Constructs a pair. This is usually written `(x, y)` instead of `Prod.mk x y`.
526   -/
527   mk ::
528   /-- The first element of a pair. -/
529   fst : α
530   /-- The second element of a pair. -/
531   snd : β
532 
533 attribute [unbox] Prod
534 
535 /--
536 A product type in which the types may be propositions, usually written `α ×' β`.
537 
538 This type is primarily used internally and as an implementation detail of proof automation. It is
539 rarely useful in hand-written code.
540 -/
541 structure PProd (α : Sort u) (β : Sort v) where
542   /-- The first element of a pair. -/
543   fst : α
544   /-- The second element of a pair. -/
545   snd : β
546 
547 /--
548 A product type in which both `α` and `β` are in the same universe.
549 
550 It is called `MProd` is because it is the *universe-monomorphic* product type.
551 -/
552 structure MProd (α β : Type u) where
553   /-- The first element of a pair. -/
554   fst : α
555   /-- The second element of a pair. -/
556   snd : β
557 
558 /--
559 `And a b`, or `a ∧ b`, is the conjunction of propositions. It can be
560 constructed and destructed like a pair: if `ha : a` and `hb : b` then
561 `⟨ha, hb⟩ : a ∧ b`, and if `h : a ∧ b` then `h.left : a` and `h.right : b`.
562 -/
563 @[pp_using_anonymous_constructor]
564 structure And (a b : Prop) : Prop where
565   /-- `And.intro : a → b → a ∧ b` is the constructor for the And operation. -/
566   intro ::
567   /-- Extract the left conjunct from a conjunction. `h : a ∧ b` then
568   `h.left`, also notated as `h.1`, is a proof of `a`. -/
569   left : a
570   /-- Extract the right conjunct from a conjunction. `h : a ∧ b` then
571   `h.right`, also notated as `h.2`, is a proof of `b`. -/
572   right : b
573 
574 /--
575 `Or a b`, or `a ∨ b`, is the disjunction of propositions. There are two
576 constructors for `Or`, called `Or.inl : a → a ∨ b` and `Or.inr : b → a ∨ b`,
577 and you can use `match` or `cases` to destruct an `Or` assumption into the
578 two cases.
579 -/
580 inductive Or (a b : Prop) : Prop where
581   /-- `Or.inl` is "left injection" into an `Or`. If `h : a` then `Or.inl h : a ∨ b`. -/
582   | inl (h : a) : Or a b
583   /-- `Or.inr` is "right injection" into an `Or`. If `h : b` then `Or.inr h : a ∨ b`. -/
584   | inr (h : b) : Or a b
585 
586 /-- Alias for `Or.inl`. -/
587 theorem Or.intro_left (b : Prop) (h : a) : Or a b :=
588   Or.inl h
589 
590 /-- Alias for `Or.inr`. -/
591 theorem Or.intro_right (a : Prop) (h : b) : Or a b :=
592   Or.inr h
593 
594 /--
595 Proof by cases on an `Or`. If `a ∨ b`, and both `a` and `b` imply
596 proposition `c`, then `c` is true.
597 -/
598 theorem Or.elim {c : Prop} (h : Or a b) (left : a → c) (right : b → c) : c :=
599   match h with
600   | Or.inl h => left h
601   | Or.inr h => right h
602 
603 theorem Or.resolve_left  (h: Or a b) (na : Not a) : b := h.elim (absurd · na) id
604 theorem Or.resolve_right (h: Or a b) (nb : Not b) : a := h.elim id (absurd · nb)
605 theorem Or.neg_resolve_left  (h : Or (Not a) b) (ha : a) : b := h.elim (absurd ha) id
606 theorem Or.neg_resolve_right (h : Or a (Not b)) (nb : b) : a := h.elim id (absurd nb)
607 
608 /--
609 The Boolean values, `true` and `false`.
610 
611 Logically speaking, this is equivalent to `Prop` (the type of propositions). The distinction is
612 public important for programming: both propositions and their proofs are erased in the code generator,
613 while `Bool` corresponds to the Boolean type in most programming languages and carries precisely one
614 bit of run-time information.
615 -/
616 inductive Bool : Type where
617   /-- The Boolean value `false`, not to be confused with the proposition `False`. -/
618   | false : Bool
619   /-- The Boolean value `true`, not to be confused with the proposition `True`. -/
620   | true : Bool
621 
622 export Bool (false true)
623 
624 /--
625 All the elements of a type that satisfy a predicate.
626 
627 `Subtype p`, usually written `{ x : α // p x }` or `{ x // p x }`, contains all elements `x : α` for
628 which `p x` is true. Its constructor is a pair of the value and the proof that it satisfies the
629 predicate. In run-time code, `{ x : α // p x }` is represented identically to `α`.
630 
631 There is a coercion from `{ x : α // p x }` to `α`, so elements of a subtype may be used where the
632 underlying type is expected.
633 
634 Examples:
635  * `{ n : Nat // n % 2 = 0 }` is the type of even numbers.
636  * `{ xs : Array String // xs.size = 5 }` is the type of arrays with five `String`s.
637  * Given `xs : List α`, `List { x : α // x ∈ xs }` is the type of lists in which all elements are
638    contained in `xs`.
639 -/
640 @[pp_using_anonymous_constructor]
641 structure Subtype {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) where
642   /--
643   The value in the underlying type that satisfies the predicate.
644   -/
645   val : α
646   /--
647   The proof that `val` satisfies the predicate `p`.
648   -/
649   property : p val
650 
651 grind_pattern Subtype.property => self.val
652 
653 set_option linter.unusedVariables.funArgs false in
654 /--
655 Gadget for optional parameter support.
656 
657 A binder like `(x : α := default)` in a declaration is syntax sugar for
658 `x : optParam α default`, and triggers the elaborator to attempt to use
659 `default` to supply the argument if it is not supplied.
660 -/
661 @[reducible] def optParam (α : Sort u) (default : α) : Sort u := α
662 
663 /--
664 Gadget for marking output parameters in type classes.
665 
666 For example, the `Membership` class is defined as:
667 ```
668 class Membership (α : outParam (Type u)) (γ : Type v)
669 ```
670 This means that whenever a typeclass goal of the form `Membership ?α ?γ` comes
671 up, Lean will wait to solve it until `?γ` is known, but then it will run
672 typeclass inference, and take the first solution it finds, for any value of `?α`,
673 which thereby determines what `?α` should be.
674 
675 This expresses that in a term like `a ∈ s`, `s` might be a `Set α` or
676 `List α` or some other type with a membership operation, and in each case
677 the "member" type `α` is determined by looking at the container type.
678 -/
679 @[reducible] def outParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α
680 
681 /--
682 Gadget for marking semi output parameters in type classes.
683 
684 Semi-output parameters influence the order in which arguments to type class
685 instances are processed.  Lean determines an order where all non-(semi-)output
686 parameters to the instance argument have to be figured out before attempting to
687 synthesize an argument (that is, they do not contain assignable metavariables
688 created during TC synthesis). This rules out instances such as `[Mul β] : Add
689 α` (because `β` could be anything). Marking a parameter as semi-output is a
690 promise that instances of the type class will always fill in a value for that
691 parameter.
692 
693 For example, the `Coe` class is defined as:
694 ```
695 class Coe (α : semiOutParam (Sort u)) (β : Sort v)
696 ```
697 This means that all `Coe` instances should provide a concrete value for `α`
698 (i.e., not an assignable metavariable). An instance like `Coe Nat Int` or `Coe
699 α (Option α)` is fine, but `Coe α Nat` is not since it does not provide a value
700 for `α`.
701 -/
702 @[reducible] def semiOutParam (α : Sort u) : Sort u := α
703 
704 set_option linter.unusedVariables.funArgs false in
705 /-- Auxiliary declaration used to implement named patterns like `x@h:p`. -/
706 @[reducible] def namedPattern {α : Sort u} (x a : α) (h : Eq x a) : α := a
707 
708 /--
709 Auxiliary axiom used to implement the `sorry` term and tactic.
710 
711 The `sorry` term/tactic expands to `sorryAx _ (synthetic := false)`.
712 It is intended for stubbing-out incomplete parts of a value or proof while still having a syntactically correct skeleton.
713 Lean will give a warning whenever a declaration uses `sorry`, so you aren't likely to miss it,
714 but you can check if a declaration depends on `sorry` either directly or indirectly by looking for `sorryAx` in the output
715 of the `#print axioms my_thm` command.
716 
717 The `synthetic` flag is false when a `sorry` is written explicitly by the user, but it is
718 set to `true` when a tactic fails to prove a goal, or if there is a type error
719 in the expression. A synthetic `sorry` acts like a regular one, except that it
720 suppresses follow-up errors in order to prevent an error from causing a cascade
721 of other errors because the desired term was not constructed.
722 -/
723 @[extern "lean_sorry", never_extract]
724 axiom sorryAx (α : Sort u) (synthetic : Bool) : α
725 
726 theorem eq_false_of_ne_true : {b : Bool} → Not (Eq b true) → Eq b false
727   | true, h => False.elim (h rfl)
728   | false, _ => rfl
729 
730 theorem eq_true_of_ne_false : {b : Bool} → Not (Eq b false) → Eq b true
731   | true, _ => rfl
732   | false, h => False.elim (h rfl)
733 
734 theorem ne_false_of_eq_true : {b : Bool} → Eq b true → Not (Eq b false)
735   | true, _  => fun h => Bool.noConfusion h
736   | false, h => Bool.noConfusion h
737 
738 theorem ne_true_of_eq_false : {b : Bool} → Eq b false → Not (Eq b true)
739   | true, h  => Bool.noConfusion h
740   | false, _ => fun h => Bool.noConfusion h
741 
742 /--
743 `Inhabited α` is a typeclass that says that `α` has a designated element,
744 called `(default : α)`. This is sometimes referred to as a "pointed type".
745 
746 This class is used by functions that need to return a value of the type
747 when called "out of domain". For example, `Array.get! arr i : α` returns
748 a value of type `α` when `arr : Array α`, but if `i` is not in range of
749 the array, it reports a panic message, but this does not halt the program,
750 so it must still return a value of type `α` (and in fact this is required
751 for logical consistency), so in this case it returns `default`.
752 -/
753 class Inhabited (α : Sort u) where
754   /-- `default` is a function that produces a "default" element of any
755   `Inhabited` type. This element does not have any particular specified
756   properties, but it is often an all-zeroes value. -/
757   default : α
758 
759 export Inhabited (default)
760 
761 /--
762 `Nonempty α` is a typeclass that says that `α` is not an empty type,
763 that is, there exists an element in the type. It differs from `Inhabited α`
764 in that `Nonempty α` is a `Prop`, which means that it does not actually carry
765 an element of `α`, only a proof that *there exists* such an element.
766 Given `Nonempty α`, you can construct an element of `α` *nonconstructively*
767 using `Classical.choice`.
768 -/
769 class inductive Nonempty (α : Sort u) : Prop where
770   /-- If `val : α`, then `α` is nonempty. -/
771   | intro (val : α) : Nonempty α
772 
773 /--
774 **The axiom of choice**. `Nonempty α` is a proof that `α` has an element,
775 but the element itself is erased. The axiom `choice` supplies a particular
776 element of `α` given only this proof.
777 
778 The textbook axiom of choice normally makes a family of choices all at once,
779 but that is implied from this formulation, because if `α : ι → Type` is a
780 family of types and `h : ∀ i, Nonempty (α i)` is a proof that they are all
781 nonempty, then `fun i => Classical.choice (h i) : ∀ i, α i` is a family of
782 chosen elements. This is actually a bit stronger than the ZFC choice axiom;
783 this is sometimes called "[global choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_of_global_choice)".
784 
785 In Lean, we use the axiom of choice to derive the law of excluded middle
786 (see `Classical.em`), so it will often show up in axiom listings where you
787 may not expect. You can use `#print axioms my_thm` to find out if a given
788 theorem depends on this or other axioms.
789 
790 This axiom can be used to construct "data", but obviously there is no algorithm
791 to compute it, so Lean will require you to mark any definition that would
792 involve executing `Classical.choice` or other axioms as `noncomputable`, and
793 will not produce any executable code for such definitions.
794 -/
795 axiom Classical.choice {α : Sort u} : Nonempty α → α
796 
797 /--
798 The elimination principle for `Nonempty α`. If `Nonempty α`, and we can
799 prove `p` given any element `x : α`, then `p` holds. Note that it is essential
800 that `p` is a `Prop` here; the version with `p` being a `Sort u` is equivalent
801 to `Classical.choice`.
802 -/
803 protected theorem Nonempty.elim {α : Sort u} {p : Prop} (h₁ : Nonempty α) (h₂ : α → p) : p :=
804   match h₁ with
805   | intro a => h₂ a
806 
807 instance {α : Sort u} [Inhabited α] : Nonempty α :=
808   ⟨default⟩
809 
810 /--
811 A variation on `Classical.choice` that uses typeclass inference to
812 infer the proof of `Nonempty α`.
813 -/
814 noncomputable def Classical.ofNonempty {α : Sort u} [Nonempty α] : α :=
815   Classical.choice inferInstance
816 
817 instance {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} [Nonempty β] : Nonempty (α → β) :=
818   Nonempty.intro fun _ => Classical.ofNonempty
819 
820 instance Pi.instNonempty {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} [(a : α) → Nonempty (β a)] :
821     Nonempty ((a : α) → β a) :=
822   Nonempty.intro fun _ => Classical.ofNonempty
823 
824 instance : Inhabited (Sort u) where
825   default := PUnit
826 
827 instance (α : Sort u) {β : Sort v} [Inhabited β] : Inhabited (α → β) where
828   default := fun _ => default
829 
830 instance Pi.instInhabited {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v} [(a : α) → Inhabited (β a)] :
831     Inhabited ((a : α) → β a) where
832   default := fun _ => default
833 
834 deriving instance Inhabited for Bool
835 
836 /--
837 Lifts a proposition or type to a higher universe level.
838 
839 `PLift α` wraps a proof or value of type `α`. The resulting type is in the next largest universe
840 after that of `α`. In particular, propositions become data.
841 
842 The related type `ULift` can be used to lift a non-proposition type by any number of levels.
843 
844 Examples:
845  * `(False : Prop)`
846  * `(PLift False : Type)`
847  * `([.up (by trivial), .up (by simp), .up (by decide)] : List (PLift True))`
848  * `(Nat : Type 0)`
849  * `(PLift Nat : Type 1)`
850 -/
851 structure PLift (α : Sort u) : Type u where
852   /-- Wraps a proof or value to increase its type's universe level by 1. -/
853   up ::
854   /-- Extracts a wrapped proof or value from a universe-lifted proposition or type. -/
855   down : α
856 
857 /-- Bijection between `α` and `PLift α` -/
858 theorem PLift.up_down {α : Sort u} (b : PLift α) : Eq (up (down b)) b := rfl
859 
860 /-- Bijection between `α` and `PLift α` -/
861 theorem PLift.down_up {α : Sort u} (a : α) : Eq (down (up a)) a := rfl
862 
863 /--
864 `NonemptyType.{u}` is the type of nonempty types in universe `u`.
865 It is mainly used in constant declarations where we wish to introduce a type
866 and simultaneously assert that it is nonempty, but otherwise make the type
867 opaque.
868 -/
869 def NonemptyType := Subtype fun α : Type u => Nonempty α
870 
871 /-- The underlying type of a `NonemptyType`. -/
872 abbrev NonemptyType.type (type : NonemptyType.{u}) : Type u :=
873   type.val
874 
875 /-- `NonemptyType` is inhabited, because `PUnit` is a nonempty type. -/
876 instance : Inhabited NonemptyType.{u} where
877   default := ⟨PUnit, ⟨⟨⟩⟩⟩
878 
879 /--
880 Lifts a type to a higher universe level.
881 
882 `ULift α` wraps a value of type `α`. Instead of occupying the same universe as `α`, which would be
883 the minimal level, it takes a further level parameter and occupies their maximum. The resulting type
884 may occupy any universe that's at least as large as that of `α`.
885 
886 The resulting universe of the lifting operator is the first parameter, and may be written explicitly
887 while allowing `α`'s level to be inferred.
888 
889 The related type `PLift` can be used to lift a proposition or type by one level.
890 
891 Examples:
892  * `(Nat : Type 0)`
893  * `(ULift Nat : Type 0)`
894  * `(ULift Nat : Type 1)`
895  * `(ULift Nat : Type 5)`
896  * `(ULift.{7} (PUnit : Type 3) : Type 7)`
897 -/
898 -- The universe variable `r` is written first so that `ULift.{r} α` can be used
899 -- when `s` can be inferred from the type of `α`.
900 structure ULift.{r, s} (α : Type s) : Type (max s r) where
901   /-- Wraps a value to increase its type's universe level. -/
902   up ::
903   /-- Extracts a wrapped value from a universe-lifted type. -/
904   down : α
905 
906 /-- Bijection between `α` and `ULift.{v} α` -/
907 theorem ULift.up_down {α : Type u} (b : ULift.{v} α) : Eq (up (down b)) b := rfl
908 
909 /-- Bijection between `α` and `ULift.{v} α` -/
910 theorem ULift.down_up {α : Type u} (a : α) : Eq (down (up.{v} a)) a := rfl
911 
912 instance [Inhabited α] : Inhabited (ULift α) where
913   default := ULift.up default
914 
915 /--
916 Lifts a type or proposition to a higher universe level.
917 
918 `PULift α` wraps a value of type `α`. It is a generalization of
919 `PLift` that allows lifting values whose type may live in `Sort s`.
920 It also subsumes `PLift`.
921 -/
922 -- The universe variable `r` is written first so that `ULift.{r} α` can be used
923 -- when `s` can be inferred from the type of `α`.
924 structure PULift.{r, s} (α : Sort s) : Sort (max s r 1) where
925   /-- Wraps a value to increase its type's universe level. -/
926   up ::
927   /-- Extracts a wrapped value from a universe-lifted type. -/
928   down : α
929 
930 /-- Bijection between `α` and `PULift.{v} α` -/
931 theorem PULift.up_down {α : Sort u} (b : PULift.{v} α) : Eq (up (down b)) b := rfl
932 
933 /-- Bijection between `α` and `PULift.{v} α` -/
934 theorem PULift.down_up {α : Sort u} (a : α) : Eq (down (up.{v} a)) a := rfl
935 
936 /--
937 Either a proof that `p` is true or a proof that `p` is false. This is equivalent to a `Bool` paired
938 with a proof that the `Bool` is `true` if and only if `p` is true.
939 
940 `Decidable` instances are primarily used via `if`-expressions and the tactic `decide`. In
941 conditional expressions, the `Decidable` instance for the proposition is used to select a branch. At
942 run time, this case distinction code is identical to that which would be generated for a
943 `Bool`-based conditional. In proofs, the tactic `decide` synthesizes an instance of `Decidable p`,
944 attempts to reduce it to `isTrue h`, and then succeeds with the proof `h` if it can.
945 
946 Because `Decidable` carries data, when writing `@[simp]` lemmas which include a `Decidable` instance
947 on the LHS, it is best to use `{_ : Decidable p}` rather than `[Decidable p]` so that non-canonical
948 instances can be found via unification rather than instance synthesis.
949 -/
950 class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
951   /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
952   | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
953   /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
954   | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p
955 
956 /--
957 Converts a decidable proposition into a `Bool`.
958 
959 If `p : Prop` is decidable, then `decide p : Bool` is the Boolean value
960 that is `true` if `p` is true and `false` if `p` is false.
961 -/
962 @[inline_if_reduce, nospecialize] def Decidable.decide (p : Prop) [h : Decidable p] : Bool :=
963   h.casesOn (fun _ => false) (fun _ => true)
964 
965 export Decidable (isTrue isFalse decide)
966 
967 /--
968 A decidable predicate.
969 
970 A predicate is decidable if the corresponding proposition is `Decidable` for each possible argument.
971 -/
972 abbrev DecidablePred {α : Sort u} (r : α → Prop) :=
973   (a : α) → Decidable (r a)
974 
975 /--
976 A decidable relation.
977 
978 A relation is decidable if the corresponding proposition is `Decidable` for all possible arguments.
979 -/
980 abbrev DecidableRel {α : Sort u} {β : Sort v} (r : α → β → Prop) :=
981   (a : α) → (b : β) → Decidable (r a b)
982 
983 /--
984 Propositional equality is `Decidable` for all elements of a type.
985 
986 In other words, an instance of `DecidableEq α` is a means of deciding the proposition `a = b` is
987 for all `a b : α`.
988 -/
989 abbrev DecidableEq (α : Sort u) :=
990   (a b : α) → Decidable (Eq a b)
991 
992 /--
993 Checks whether two terms of a type are equal using the type's `DecidableEq` instance.
994 -/
995 def decEq {α : Sort u} [inst : DecidableEq α] (a b : α) : Decidable (Eq a b) :=
996   inst a b
997 
998 set_option linter.unusedVariables false in
999 theorem decide_eq_true : [inst : Decidable p] → p → Eq (decide p) true
1000   | isTrue  _, _   => rfl
1001   | isFalse h₁, h₂ => absurd h₂ h₁
1002 
1003 theorem decide_eq_false : [Decidable p] → Not p → Eq (decide p) false
1004   | isTrue  h₁, h₂ => absurd h₁ h₂
1005   | isFalse _, _   => rfl
1006 
1007 theorem of_decide_eq_true [inst : Decidable p] : Eq (decide p) true → p := fun h =>
1008   match (generalizing := false) inst with
1009   | isTrue  h₁ => h₁
1010   | isFalse h₁ => absurd h (ne_true_of_eq_false (decide_eq_false h₁))
1011 
1012 theorem of_decide_eq_false [inst : Decidable p] : Eq (decide p) false → Not p := fun h =>
1013   match (generalizing := false) inst with
1014   | isTrue  h₁ => absurd h (ne_false_of_eq_true (decide_eq_true h₁))
1015   | isFalse h₁ => h₁
1016 
1017 theorem of_decide_eq_self_eq_true [inst : DecidableEq α] (a : α) : Eq (decide (Eq a a)) true :=
1018   match (generalizing := false) inst a a with
1019   | isTrue  _  => rfl
1020   | isFalse h₁ => absurd rfl h₁
1021 
1022 /--
1023 Decides whether two Booleans are equal.
1024 
1025 This function should normally be called via the `DecidableEq Bool` instance that it exists to
1026 support.
1027 -/
1028 @[inline] def Bool.decEq (a b : Bool) : Decidable (Eq a b) :=
1029    match a, b with
1030    | false, false => isTrue rfl
1031    | false, true  => isFalse (fun h => Bool.noConfusion h)
1032    | true, false  => isFalse (fun h => Bool.noConfusion h)
1033    | true, true   => isTrue rfl
1034 
1035 @[inline] instance : DecidableEq Bool :=
1036    Bool.decEq
1037 
1038 /--
1039 `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
1040 `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
1041 is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
1042 axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
1043 programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
1044 `==` and `=` coincide.
1045 
1046 Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
1047 and the "more constant" term on the right.
1048 -/
1049 class BEq (α : Type u) where
1050   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
1051   beq : α → α → Bool
1052 
1053 open BEq (beq)
1054 
1055 instance (priority := 500) [DecidableEq α] : BEq α where
1056   beq a b := decide (Eq a b)
1057 
1058 
1059 /--
1060 "Dependent" if-then-else, normally written via the notation `if h : c then t(h) else e(h)`,
1061 is sugar for `dite c (fun h => t(h)) (fun h => e(h))`, and it is the same as
1062 `if c then t else e` except that `t` is allowed to depend on a proof `h : c`,
1063 and `e` can depend on `h : ¬c`. (Both branches use the same name for the hypothesis,
1064 even though it has different types in the two cases.)
1065 
1066 We use this to be able to communicate the if-then-else condition to the branches.
1067 For example, `Array.get arr i h` expects a proof `h : i < arr.size` in order to
1068 avoid a bounds check, so you can write `if h : i < arr.size then arr.get i h else ...`
1069 to avoid the bounds check inside the if branch. (Of course in this case we have only
1070 lifted the check into an explicit `if`, but we could also use this proof multiple times
1071 or derive `i < arr.size` from some other proposition that we are checking in the `if`.)
1072 -/
1073 @[macro_inline] def dite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t : c → α) (e : Not c → α) : α :=
1074   h.casesOn e t
1075 
1076 /-! # if-then-else -/
1077 
1078 /--
1079 `if c then t else e` is notation for `ite c t e`, "if-then-else", which decides to
1080 return `t` or `e` depending on whether `c` is true or false. The explicit argument
1081 `c : Prop` does not have any actual computational content, but there is an additional
1082 `[Decidable c]` argument synthesized by typeclass inference which actually
1083 determines how to evaluate `c` to true or false. Write `if h : c then t else e`
1084 instead for a "dependent if-then-else" `dite`, which allows `t`/`e` to use the fact
1085 that `c` is true/false.
1086 -/
1087 /-
1088 Because Lean uses a strict (call-by-value) evaluation strategy, the signature of this
1089 function is problematic in that it would require `t` and `e` to be evaluated before
1090 calling the `ite` function, which would cause both sides of the `if` to be evaluated.
1091 Even if the result is discarded, this would be a big performance problem,
1092 and is undesirable for users in any case. To resolve this, `ite` is marked as
1093 `@[macro_inline]`, which means that it is unfolded during code generation, and
1094 the definition of the function uses `fun _ => t` and `fun _ => e` so this recovers
1095 the expected "lazy" behavior of `if`: the `t` and `e` arguments delay evaluation
1096 until `c` is known.
1097 -/
1098 @[macro_inline] def ite {α : Sort u} (c : Prop) [h : Decidable c] (t e : α) : α :=
1099   h.casesOn (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
1100 
1101 @[macro_inline] instance {p q} [dp : Decidable p] [dq : Decidable q] : Decidable (And p q) :=
1102   match dp with
1103   | isTrue  hp =>
1104     match dq with
1105     | isTrue hq  => isTrue ⟨hp, hq⟩
1106     | isFalse hq => isFalse (fun h => hq (And.right h))
1107   | isFalse hp =>
1108     isFalse (fun h => hp (And.left h))
1109 
1110 @[macro_inline] instance [dp : Decidable p] [dq : Decidable q] : Decidable (Or p q) :=
1111   match dp with
1112   | isTrue  hp => isTrue (Or.inl hp)
1113   | isFalse hp =>
1114     match dq with
1115     | isTrue hq  => isTrue (Or.inr hq)
1116     | isFalse hq =>
1117       isFalse fun h => match h with
1118         | Or.inl h => hp h
1119         | Or.inr h => hq h
1120 
1121 @[inline]
1122 instance [dp : Decidable p] : Decidable (Not p) :=
1123   match dp with
1124   | isTrue hp  => isFalse (absurd hp)
1125   | isFalse hp => isTrue hp
1126 
1127 /-! # Boolean operators -/
1128 
1129 /--
1130 The conditional function.
1131 
1132 `cond c x y` is the same as `if c then x else y`, but optimized for a Boolean condition rather than
1133 a decidable proposition. It can also be written using the notation `bif c then x else y`.
1134 
1135 Just like `ite`, `cond` is declared `@[macro_inline]`, which causes applications of `cond` to be
1136 unfolded. As a result, `x` and `y` are not evaluated at runtime until one of them is selected, and
1137 only the selected branch is evaluated.
1138 -/
1139 @[macro_inline] def cond {α : Sort u} (c : Bool) (x y : α) : α :=
1140   match c with
1141   | true  => x
1142   | false => y
1143 
1144 
1145 /--
1146 The dependent conditional function, in which each branch is provided with a local assumption about
1147 the condition's value. This allows the value to be used in proofs as well as for control flow.
1148 
1149 `dcond c (fun h => x) (fun h => y)` is the same as `if h : c then x else y`, but optimized for a
1150 Boolean condition rather than a decidable proposition. Unlike the non-dependent version `cond`,
1151 there is no special notation for `dcond`.
1152 
1153 Just like `ite`, `dite`, and `cond`, `dcond` is declared `@[macro_inline]`, which causes
1154 applications of `dcond` to be unfolded. As a result, `x` and `y` are not evaluated at runtime until
1155 one of them is selected, and only the selected branch is evaluated. `dcond` is intended for
1156 metaprogramming use, rather than for use in verified programs, so behavioral lemmas are not
1157 provided.
1158 -/
1159 @[macro_inline]
1160 protected def Bool.dcond {α : Sort u} (c : Bool) (x : Eq c true → α) (y : Eq c false → α) : α :=
1161   match c with
1162   | true  => x rfl
1163   | false => y rfl
1164 
1165 /--
1166 Boolean “or”, also known as disjunction. `or x y` can be written `x || y`.
1167 
1168 The corresponding propositional connective is `Or : Prop → Prop → Prop`, written with the `∨`
1169 operator.
1170 
1171 The Boolean `or` is a `@[macro_inline]` function in order to give it short-circuiting evaluation:
1172 if `x` is `true` then `y` is not evaluated at runtime.
1173 -/
1174 @[macro_inline] def Bool.or (x y : Bool) : Bool :=
1175   match x with
1176   | true  => true
1177   | false => y
1178 
1179 /--
1180 Boolean “and”, also known as conjunction. `and x y` can be written `x && y`.
1181 
1182 The corresponding propositional connective is `And : Prop → Prop → Prop`, written with the `∧`
1183 operator.
1184 
1185 The Boolean `and` is a `@[macro_inline]` function in order to give it short-circuiting evaluation:
1186 if `x` is `false` then `y` is not evaluated at runtime.
1187 -/
1188 @[macro_inline] def Bool.and (x y : Bool) : Bool :=
1189   match x with
1190   | false => false
1191   | true  => y
1192 
1193 /--
1194 Boolean negation, also known as Boolean complement. `not x` can be written `!x`.
1195 
1196 This is a function that maps the value `true` to `false` and the value `false` to `true`. The
1197 propositional connective is `Not : Prop → Prop`.
1198 -/
1199 @[inline] def Bool.not : Bool → Bool
1200   | true  => false
1201   | false => true
1202 
1203 export Bool (or and not)
1204 
1205 set_option genCtorIdx false in
1206 /--
1207 The natural numbers, starting at zero.
1208 
1209 This type is special-cased by both the kernel and the compiler, and overridden with an efficient
1210 implementation. Both use a fast arbitrary-precision arithmetic library (usually
1211 [GMP](https://gmplib.org/)); at runtime, `Nat` values that are sufficiently small are unboxed.
1212 -/
1213 @[suggest_for ℕ]
1214 inductive Nat where
1215   /--
1216   Zero, the smallest natural number.
1217 
1218   Using `Nat.zero` explicitly should usually be avoided in favor of the literal `0`, which is the
1219   [simp normal form](lean-manual://section/simp-normal-forms).
1220   -/
1221   | zero : Nat
1222   /--
1223   The successor of a natural number `n`.
1224 
1225   Using `Nat.succ n` should usually be avoided in favor of `n + 1`, which is the [simp normal
1226   form](lean-manual://section/simp-normal-forms).
1227   -/
1228   | succ (n : Nat) : Nat
1229 
1230 instance : Inhabited Nat where
1231   default := Nat.zero
1232 
1233 /--
1234 The class `OfNat α n` powers the numeric literal parser. If you write
1235 `37 : α`, Lean will attempt to synthesize `OfNat α 37`, and will generate
1236 the term `(OfNat.ofNat 37 : α)`.
1237 
1238 There is a bit of infinite regress here since the desugaring apparently
1239 still contains a literal `37` in it. The type of expressions contains a
1240 primitive constructor for "raw natural number literals", which you can directly
1241 access using the macro `nat_lit 37`. Raw number literals are always of type `Nat`.
1242 So it would be more correct to say that Lean looks for an instance of
1243 `OfNat α (nat_lit 37)`, and it generates the term `(OfNat.ofNat (nat_lit 37) : α)`.
1244 -/
1245 class OfNat (α : Type u) (_ : Nat) where
1246   /-- The `OfNat.ofNat` function is automatically inserted by the parser when
1247   the user writes a numeric literal like `1 : α`. Implementations of this
1248   typeclass can therefore customize the behavior of `n : α` based on `n` and
1249   `α`. -/
1250   ofNat : α
1251 
1252 @[default_instance 100] /- low prio -/
1253 instance instOfNatNat (n : Nat) : OfNat Nat n where
1254   ofNat := n
1255 
1256 /-- `LE α` is the typeclass which supports the notation `x ≤ y` where `x y : α`.-/
1257 class LE (α : Type u) where
1258   /-- The less-equal relation: `x ≤ y` -/
1259   le : α → α → Prop
1260 
1261 /-- `LT α` is the typeclass which supports the notation `x < y` where `x y : α`.-/
1262 class LT (α : Type u) where
1263   /-- The less-than relation: `x < y` -/
1264   lt : α → α → Prop
1265 
1266 /-- `a ≥ b` is an abbreviation for `b ≤ a`. -/
1267 @[reducible] def GE.ge {α : Type u} [LE α] (a b : α) : Prop := LE.le b a
1268 /-- `a > b` is an abbreviation for `b < a`. -/
1269 @[reducible] def GT.gt {α : Type u} [LT α] (a b : α) : Prop := LT.lt b a
1270 
1271 /-- Abbreviation for `DecidableRel (· < · : α → α → Prop)`. -/
1272 abbrev DecidableLT (α : Type u) [LT α] := DecidableRel (LT.lt : α → α → Prop)
1273 /-- Abbreviation for `DecidableRel (· ≤ · : α → α → Prop)`. -/
1274 abbrev DecidableLE (α : Type u) [LE α] := DecidableRel (LE.le : α → α → Prop)
1275 
1276 /--
1277 An overloaded operation to find the greater of two values of type `α`.
1278 -/
1279 class Max (α : Type u) where
1280   /-- Returns the greater of its two arguments. -/
1281   max : α → α → α
1282 
1283 export Max (max)
1284 
1285 /--
1286 Constructs a `Max` instance from a decidable `≤` operation.
1287 -/
1288 -- Marked inline so that `min x y + max x y` can be optimized to a single branch.
1289 @[inline, implicit_reducible]
1290 def maxOfLe [LE α] [DecidableRel (@LE.le α _)] : Max α where
1291   max x y := ite (LE.le x y) y x
1292 
1293 /--
1294 An overloaded operation to find the lesser of two values of type `α`.
1295 -/
1296 class Min (α : Type u) where
1297   /-- Returns the lesser of its two arguments. -/
1298   min : α → α → α
1299 
1300 export Min (min)
1301 
1302 /--
1303 Constructs a `Min` instance from a decidable `≤` operation.
1304 -/
1305 -- Marked inline so that `min x y + max x y` can be optimized to a single branch.
1306 @[inline, implicit_reducible]
1307 def minOfLe [LE α] [DecidableRel (@LE.le α _)] : Min α where
1308   min x y := ite (LE.le x y) x y

1310 /--
1311 Transitive chaining of proofs, used e.g. by `calc`.
1312 
1313 It takes two relations `r` and `s` as "input", and produces an "output"
1314 relation `t`, with the property that `r a b` and `s b c` implies `t a c`.
1315 The `calc` tactic uses this so that when it sees a chain with `a ≤ b` and `b < c`
1316 it knows that this should be a proof of `a < c` because there is an instance
1317 `Trans (·≤·) (·<·) (·<·)`.
1318 -/
1319 class Trans (r : α → β → Sort u) (s : β → γ → Sort v) (t : outParam (α → γ → Sort w)) where
1320   /-- Compose two proofs by transitivity, generalized over the relations involved. -/
1321   trans : r a b → s b c → t a c
1322 
1323 export Trans (trans)
1324 
1325 instance (r : α → γ → Sort u) : Trans Eq r r where
1326   trans heq h' := heq ▸ h'
1327 
1328 instance (r : α → β → Sort u) : Trans r Eq r where
1329   trans h' heq := heq ▸ h'
1330 
1331 /--
1332 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous addition.
1333 This enables the notation `a + b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1334 -/
1335 class HAdd (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1336   /-- `a + b` computes the sum of `a` and `b`.
1337   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1338   hAdd : α → β → γ
1339 
1340 /--
1341 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous subtraction.
1342 This enables the notation `a - b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1343 -/
1344 class HSub (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1345   /-- `a - b` computes the difference of `a` and `b`.
1346   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
1347   * For natural numbers, this operator saturates at 0: `a - b = 0` when `a ≤ b`. -/
1348   hSub : α → β → γ
1349 
1350 /--
1351 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous multiplication.
1352 This enables the notation `a * b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1353 -/
1354 class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1355   /-- `a * b` computes the product of `a` and `b`.
1356   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1357   hMul : α → β → γ
1358 
1359 /--
1360 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous division.
1361 This enables the notation `a / b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1362 -/
1363 class HDiv (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1364   /-- `a / b` computes the result of dividing `a` by `b`.
1365   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
1366   * For most types like `Nat`, `Int`, `Rat`, `Real`, `a / 0` is defined to be `0`.
1367   * For `Nat`, `a / b` rounds downwards.
1368   * For `Int`, `a / b` rounds downwards if `b` is positive or upwards if `b` is negative.
1369     It is implemented as `Int.ediv`, the unique function satisfying
1370     `a % b + b * (a / b) = a` and `0 ≤ a % b < natAbs b` for `b ≠ 0`.
1371     Other rounding conventions are available using the functions
1372     `Int.fdiv` (floor rounding) and `Int.tdiv` (truncation rounding).
1373   * For `Float`, `a / 0` follows the IEEE 754 semantics for division,
1374     usually resulting in `inf` or `nan`. -/
1375   hDiv : α → β → γ
1376 
1377 /--
1378 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous modulo / remainder.
1379 This enables the notation `a % b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1380 -/
1381 class HMod (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1382   /-- `a % b` computes the remainder upon dividing `a` by `b`.
1383   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
1384   * For `Nat` and `Int` it satisfies `a % b + b * (a / b) = a`,
1385     and `a % 0` is defined to be `a`. -/
1386   hMod : α → β → γ
1387 
1388 /--
1389 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous exponentiation.
1390 This enables the notation `a ^ b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1391 -/
1392 class HPow (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1393   /-- `a ^ b` computes `a` to the power of `b`.
1394   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1395   hPow : α → β → γ
1396 
1397 /--
1398 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous scalar multiplication.
1399 This enables the notation `a • b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1400 
1401 It is assumed to represent a left action in some sense.
1402 The notation `a • b` is augmented with a macro (below) to have it elaborate as a left action.
1403 Only the `b` argument participates in the elaboration algorithm: the algorithm uses the type of `b`
1404 when calculating the type of the surrounding arithmetic expression
1405 and it tries to insert coercions into `b` to get some `b'`
1406 such that `a • b'` has the same type as `b'`.
1407 See the module documentation near the macro for more details.
1408 -/
1409 class HSMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1410   /-- `a • b` computes the product of `a` and `b`.
1411   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent, but it is intended to be used for left actions. -/
1412   hSMul : α → β → γ
1413 
1414 /--
1415 The notation typeclass for heterogeneous append.
1416 This enables the notation `a ++ b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1417 -/
1418 class HAppend (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1419   /-- `a ++ b` is the result of concatenation of `a` and `b`, usually read "append".
1420   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1421   hAppend : α → β → γ
1422 
1423 /--
1424 The typeclass behind the notation `a <|> b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1425 Because `b` is "lazy" in this notation, it is passed as `Unit → β` to the
1426 implementation so it can decide when to evaluate it.
1427 -/
1428 class HOrElse (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1429   /-- `a <|> b` executes `a` and returns the result, unless it fails in which
1430   case it executes and returns `b`. Because `b` is not always executed, it
1431   is passed as a thunk so it can be forced only when needed.
1432   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1433   hOrElse : α → (Unit → β) → γ
1434 
1435 /--
1436 The typeclass behind the notation `a >> b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1437 Because `b` is "lazy" in this notation, it is passed as `Unit → β` to the
1438 implementation so it can decide when to evaluate it.
1439 -/
1440 class HAndThen (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1441   /-- `a >> b` executes `a`, ignores the result, and then executes `b`.
1442   If `a` fails then `b` is not executed. Because `b` is not always executed, it
1443   is passed as a thunk so it can be forced only when needed.
1444   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1445   hAndThen : α → (Unit → β) → γ
1446 
1447 /-- The typeclass behind the notation `a &&& b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`. -/
1448 class HAnd (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1449   /-- `a &&& b` computes the bitwise AND of `a` and `b`.
1450   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1451   hAnd : α → β → γ
1452 
1453 /-- The typeclass behind the notation `a ^^^ b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`. -/
1454 class HXor (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1455   /-- `a ^^^ b` computes the bitwise XOR of `a` and `b`.
1456   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1457   hXor : α → β → γ
1458 
1459 /-- The typeclass behind the notation `a ||| b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`. -/
1460 class HOr (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1461   /-- `a ||| b` computes the bitwise OR of `a` and `b`.
1462   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/
1463   hOr : α → β → γ
1464 
1465 /-- The typeclass behind the notation `a <<< b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`. -/
1466 class HShiftLeft (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1467   /-- `a <<< b` computes `a` shifted to the left by `b` places.
1468   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
1469   * On `Nat`, this is equivalent to `a * 2 ^ b`.
1470   * On `UInt8` and other fixed width unsigned types, this is the same but
1471     truncated to the bit width. -/
1472   hShiftLeft : α → β → γ
1473 
1474 /-- The typeclass behind the notation `a >>> b : γ` where `a : α`, `b : β`. -/
1475 class HShiftRight (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : outParam (Type w)) where
1476   /-- `a >>> b` computes `a` shifted to the right by `b` places.
1477   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent.
1478   * On `Nat` and fixed width unsigned types like `UInt8`,
1479     this is equivalent to `a / 2 ^ b`. -/
1480   hShiftRight : α → β → γ

1512   /-- `-a` computes the negative or opposite of `a`.

1518   /-- `a / b` computes the result of dividing `a` by `b`. See `HDiv`. -/
1519   div : α → α → α

1522 The notation typeclass for inverses.

1526   /-- `a⁻¹` computes the inverse of `a`.
1527   The meaning of this notation is type-dependent. -/

1530 /-- The homogeneous version of `HMod`: `a % b : α` where `a b : α`. -/

1535 /-- Notation typeclass for the `∣` operation (typed as `\|`), which represents divisibility. -/
1536 class Dvd (α : Type _) where

1540 /--
1541 The homogeneous version of `HPow`: `a ^ b : α` where `a : α`, `b : β`.
1542 (The right argument is not the same as the left since we often want this even
1543 in the homogeneous case.)
1544 
1545 Types can choose to subscribe to particular defaulting behavior by providing
1546 an instance to either `NatPow` or `HomogeneousPow`:
1547 - `NatPow` is for types whose exponents is preferentially a `Nat`.
1548 - `HomogeneousPow` is for types whose base and exponent are preferentially the same.
1549 -/
1550 class Pow (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
1551   /-- `a ^ b` computes `a` to the power of `b`. See `HPow`. -/
1552   pow : α → β → α
1553 
1554 /-- The homogeneous version of `Pow` where the exponent is a `Nat`.
1555 The purpose of this class is that it provides a default `Pow` instance,
1556 which can be used to specialize the exponent to `Nat` during elaboration.
1557 
1558 For example, if `x ^ 2` should preferentially elaborate with `2 : Nat` then `x`'s type should
1559 provide an instance for this class. -/
1560 class NatPow (α : Type u) where
1561   /-- `a ^ n` computes `a` to the power of `n` where `n : Nat`. See `Pow`. -/
1562   protected pow : α → Nat → α
1563 
1564 /-- The completely homogeneous version of `Pow` where the exponent has the same type as the base.
1565 The purpose of this class is that it provides a default `Pow` instance,
1566 which can be used to specialize the exponent to have the same type as the base's type during elaboration.
1567 This is to say, a type should provide an instance for this class in case `x ^ y` should be elaborated
1568 with both `x` and `y` having the same type.
1569 
1570 For example, the `Float` type provides an instance of this class, which causes expressions
1571 such as `(2.2 ^ 2.2 : Float)` to elaborate. -/
1572 class HomogeneousPow (α : Type u) where
1573   /-- `a ^ b` computes `a` to the power of `b` where `a` and `b` both have the same type. -/
1574   protected pow : α → α → α

2128 /--
2129 Division of natural numbers, discarding the remainder. Division by `0` returns `0`. Usually accessed
2130 via the `/` operator.

2132 This operation is sometimes called “floor division.”
2133 
2134 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation. This definition is
2135 the logical model.

2139  * `21 / 5 = 4`

2146     let rec
2147       go (fuel : Nat) (x : Nat) (hfuel : LT.lt x fuel) : Nat :=
2148       match fuel with
2149       | succ fuel =>
2150         dite (LE.le y x)
2151           (fun h => HAdd.hAdd (go fuel (HSub.hSub x y) (div_rec_fuel_lemma hy h hfuel)) 1)
2152           (fun _ => 0)
2153       termination_by structural fuel
2154     go (succ x) x (Nat.lt_succ_self _))
2155     (fun _ => 0)

2160 /--

2163 than an error.

2166 natural numbers, but it does not have some convenient [definitional
2167 reductions](lean-manual://section/type-system) when the `Nat`s contain free variables. The wrapper
2168 `Nat.mod` handles those cases specially and then calls `Nat.modCore`.

2171 logical model.

2175   dite (LT.lt 0 y)

2177       let rec
2178         go (fuel : Nat) (x : Nat) (hfuel : LT.lt x fuel) : Nat :=
2179         match fuel with
2180         | succ fuel =>
2181           dite (LE.le y x)
2182             (fun h => go fuel (HSub.hSub x y) (div_rec_fuel_lemma hy h hfuel))

2206 /--
2207 The modulo operator, which computes the remainder when dividing one natural number by another.
2208 Usually accessed via the `%` operator. When the divisor is `0`, the result is the dividend rather
2209 than an error.
2210 
2211 `Nat.mod` is a wrapper around `Nat.modCore` that special-cases two situations, giving better
2212 definitional reductions:
2213  * `Nat.mod 0 m` should reduce to `m`, for all terms `m : Nat`.
2214  * `Nat.mod n (m + n + 1)` should reduce to `n` for concrete `Nat` literals `n`.
2215 
2216 These reductions help `Fin n` literals work well, because the `OfNat` instance for `Fin` uses
2217 `Nat.mod`. In particular, `(0 : Fin (n + 1)).val` should reduce definitionally to `0`. `Nat.modCore`
2218 can handle all numbers, but its definitional reductions are not as convenient.
2219 
2220 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation. This definition is the
2221 logical model.
2222 
2223 Examples:
2224  * `7 % 2 = 1`
2225  * `9 % 3 = 0`
2226  * `5 % 7 = 5`
2227  * `5 % 0 = 5`
2228  * `show ∀ (n : Nat), 0 % n = 0 from fun _ => rfl`
2229  * `show ∀ (m : Nat), 5 % (m + 6) = 5 from fun _ => rfl`
2230 -/
2231 @[extern "lean_nat_mod"]
2232 protected def Nat.mod : @& Nat → @& Nat → Nat
2233   /-
2234   Nat.modCore is defined with fuel and thus does not reduce with open terms very well.
2235   Nevertheless it is desirable for trivial `Nat.mod` calculations, namely
2236   * `Nat.mod 0 m` for all `m`
2237   * `Nat.mod n (m + n + 1)` for concrete literals `n`,
2238   to reduce definitionally.
2239   This property is desirable for `Fin n` literals, as it means `(ofNat 0 : Fin n).val = 0` by
2240   definition.
2241    -/
2242   | 0, _ => 0
2243   | n@(succ _), m => ite (LE.le m n) (Nat.modCore n m) n
2244 
2245 instance Nat.instMod : Mod Nat := ⟨Nat.mod⟩

2247 theorem Nat.mod_lt : (x : Nat) →  {y : Nat} → (hy : LT.lt 0 y) → LT.lt (HMod.hMod x y) y
2248   | 0, succ _, _ => Nat.zero_lt_succ _
2249   | succ n, m, hm =>
2250     show LT.lt (ite (LE.le m (succ n)) (Nat.modCore (succ n) m) (succ n)) _ from
2251       match Nat.decLe m (succ n) with
2252       | .isTrue _ => Nat.modCore_lt hm
2253       | .isFalse h => Nat.lt_of_not_le h

2609 `DecidableEq UInt32` instance.
2610 
2611 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation.
2612 
2613 Examples:
2614  * `UInt32.decEq 123 123 = .isTrue rfl`
2615  * `(if (6 : UInt32) = 7 then "yes" else "no") = "no"`
2616  * `show (7 : UInt32) = 7 by decide`
2617 -/
2618 @[extern "lean_uint32_dec_eq"]
2619 def UInt32.decEq (a b : UInt32) : Decidable (Eq a b) :=
2620   match a, b with
2621   | ⟨n⟩, ⟨m⟩ =>
2622     dite (Eq n m) (fun h => isTrue (h ▸ rfl)) (fun h => isFalse (fun h' => UInt32.noConfusion h' (fun h' => absurd h' h)))
2623 
2624 instance : DecidableEq UInt32 := UInt32.decEq
2625 
2626 instance : Inhabited UInt32 where
2627   default := UInt32.ofNatLT 0 (of_decide_eq_true rfl)
2628 
2629 instance : LT UInt32 where
2630   lt a b := LT.lt a.toBitVec b.toBitVec
2631 
2632 instance : LE UInt32 where
2633   le a b := LE.le a.toBitVec b.toBitVec
2634 
2635 /--
2636 Decides whether one 8-bit unsigned integer is strictly less than another. Usually accessed via the
2637 `DecidableLT UInt32` instance.
2638 
2639 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation.
2640 
2641 Examples:
2642  * `(if (6 : UInt32) < 7 then "yes" else "no") = "yes"`
2643  * `(if (5 : UInt32) < 5 then "yes" else "no") = "no"`
2644  * `show ¬((7 : UInt32) < 7) by decide`
2645 -/
2646 @[extern "lean_uint32_dec_lt", implicit_reducible]
2647 def UInt32.decLt (a b : UInt32) : Decidable (LT.lt a b) :=
2648   inferInstanceAs (Decidable (LT.lt a.toBitVec b.toBitVec))
2649 
2650 /--
2651 Decides whether one 32-bit signed integer is less than or equal to another. Usually accessed via the
2652 `DecidableLE UInt32` instance.
2653 
2654 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation.
2655 
2656 Examples:
2657  * `(if (15 : UInt32) ≤ 15 then "yes" else "no") = "yes"`
2658  * `(if (15 : UInt32) ≤ 5 then "yes" else "no") = "no"`
2659  * `(if (5 : UInt32) ≤ 15 then "yes" else "no") = "yes"`
2660  * `show (7 : UInt32) ≤ 7 by decide`
2661 -/
2662 @[extern "lean_uint32_dec_le", implicit_reducible]
2663 def UInt32.decLe (a b : UInt32) : Decidable (LE.le a b) :=
2664   inferInstanceAs (Decidable (LE.le a.toBitVec b.toBitVec))
2665 
2666 attribute [instance] UInt32.decLt UInt32.decLe
2667 
2668 instance : Max UInt32 := maxOfLe
2669 instance : Min UInt32 := minOfLe

2671 /-- The number of distinct values representable by `UInt64`, that is, `2^64 = 18446744073709551616`. -/
2672 abbrev UInt64.size : Nat := 18446744073709551616
2673 
2674 /--
2675 Unsigned 64-bit integers.
2676 
2677 This type has special support in the compiler so it can be represented by an unboxed 64-bit value
2678 rather than wrapping a `BitVec 64`.
2679 -/
2680 structure UInt64 where
2681   /--
2682   Creates a `UInt64` from a `BitVec 64`. This function is overridden with a native implementation.
2683   -/
2684   ofBitVec ::
2685   /--
2686   Unpacks a `UInt64` into a `BitVec 64`. This function is overridden with a native implementation.
2687   -/
2688   toBitVec : BitVec 64

2691 attribute [extern "lean_uint64_to_nat"] UInt64.toBitVec

2697 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation.

2699 @[extern "lean_uint64_of_nat"]
2700 def UInt64.ofNatLT (n : @& Nat) (h : LT.lt n UInt64.size) : UInt64 where
2701   toBitVec := BitVec.ofNatLT n h

2705 /--
2706 Decides whether two 64-bit unsigned integers are equal. Usually accessed via the
2707 `DecidableEq UInt64` instance.

2709 This function is overridden at runtime with an efficient implementation.
2710 
2711 Examples:
2712  * `UInt64.decEq 123 123 = .isTrue rfl`
2713  * `(if (6 : UInt64) = 7 then "yes" else "no") = "no"`
2714  * `show (7 : UInt64) = 7 by decide`
2715 -/
2716 @[extern "lean_uint64_dec_eq"]
2717 def UInt64.decEq (a b : UInt64) : Decidable (Eq a b) :=
2718   match a, b with
2719   | ⟨n⟩, ⟨m⟩ =>
2720     dite (Eq n m)
2721       (fun h => isTrue (h ▸ rfl))
2722       (fun h => isFalse (fun h' => UInt64.noConfusion h' (fun h' => absurd h' h)))
2723 
2724 instance : DecidableEq UInt64 := UInt64.decEq

2726 instance : Inhabited UInt64 where

2729 /-- The number of distinct values representable by `USize`, that is, `2^System.Platform.numBits`. -/
2730 abbrev USize.size : Nat := (hPow 2 System.Platform.numBits)
2731 
2732 theorem USize.size_eq : Or (Eq USize.size 4294967296) (Eq USize.size 18446744073709551616) :=
2733   show Or (Eq (hPow 2 System.Platform.numBits) 4294967296) (Eq (hPow 2 System.Platform.numBits) 18446744073709551616) from
2734   match System.Platform.numBits, System.Platform.numBits_eq with
2735   | _, Or.inl rfl => Or.inl (of_decide_eq_true rfl)
2736   | _, Or.inr rfl => Or.inr (of_decide_eq_true rfl)
2737 
2738 theorem USize.size_pos : LT.lt 0 USize.size :=
2739   match USize.size, USize.size_eq with
2740   | _, Or.inl rfl => of_decide_eq_true rfl
2741   | _, Or.inr rfl => of_decide_eq_true rfl
2742 
2743 /--
2744 Unsigned integers that are the size of a word on the platform's architecture.

2746 On a 32-bit architecture, `USize` is equivalent to `UInt32`. On a 64-bit machine, it is equivalent
2747 to `UInt64`.
2748 -/
2749 structure USize where
2750   /--
2751   Creates a `USize` from a `BitVec System.Platform.numBits`. This function is overridden with a
2752   native implementation.
2753   -/
2754   ofBitVec ::
2755   /--
2756   Unpacks a `USize` into a `BitVec System.Platform.numBits`. This function is overridden with a native
2757   implementation.
2758   -/
2759   toBitVec : BitVec System.Platform.numBits

2762 attribute [extern "lean_usize_to_nat"] USize.toBitVec

2772   toBitVec := BitVec.ofNatLT n h
